linkage.caveat: Rates describe trials that posted a usable result. A trial counted as having no identified publication may still be published; matching has false negatives.

publication_model.note: Outcome is whether a publication was identified. A positive log_hr coefficient means trials with weaker treatment effects were MORE likely to be linked to a publication; a negative one means they were less likely. Small cohorts give wide intervals -- read the interval, not the point estimate.

priors.interpretation: Adding 21 registry-only trial(s) moved the pooled hazard ratio toward the null (from 0.725 to 0.771). In this cohort the identified literature shows a larger treatment effect than the registry record as a whole.
priors.caveat: This compares only results that are observable. Trials with neither a publication nor a posted result are not included here; their influence is explored through sensitivity analysis instead.

literature_only.label: literature-only
literature_only.note: Small trials report systematically stronger effects than large ones (intercept -2.74, p < 0.001). That is the shape publication selection leaves.

registry_aware.label: registry-aware
registry_aware.note: Small trials report systematically stronger effects than large ones (intercept -2.19, p < 0.001). That is the shape publication selection leaves.

placement.note: 16 of the 21 registry-only trials are less precise than the median published trial, and 17 report a weaker effect than the pooled estimate.

funnel.note: Each point is one trial with a poolable hazard ratio; trials with no usable estimate are absent, not at the null. The funnel is a pseudo 95% region around the registry-aware pooled estimate. Asymmetry has causes other than publication selection, such as genuine small-study effects.

rows.label: Your assumption
rows.note: The design as proposed, by construction hitting its power target.

consequence.summary: A trial sized for HR 0.65 needs 170 events. If the registry-aware estimate of HR 0.77 is closer to the truth, those 170 events deliver 40% power rather than 80%, and reaching the target would take 465 events (+295 more).

design.method: Schoenfeld approximation for the log-rank test, 1:1 allocation. Event counts drive the calculation; participant counts appear only when an overall event probability is supplied.

sensitivity.note: Each of the 309 trial(s) with no identified publication and no posted result is represented by one pseudo-trial at the assumed hazard ratio, given the median precision of the 91 trial(s) that did report. These are assumptions under test, not findings.

backtest.verdict: At a target of 80%, literature-only covered 84% and registry-aware covered 81%. Mean absolute error on log(HR) was 0.338 versus 0.323. Literature-only predicted a stronger effect than the held-out trials delivered (bias -0.041 on log(HR)); registry-aware was closer to unbiased (+0.021). That direction is what publication selection predicts. Registry-aware evidence was better calibrated and no less accurate. With a cohort this size, a few folds move these numbers materially; treat the comparison as indicative rather than conclusive.
backtest.method: Leave-one-out. Each held-out trial is predicted from a random-effects pool of the remaining trials, using a prediction interval for the next trial rather than a confidence interval for the mean.
